text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Front matter (Foreword, Key Takeaways, Abbreviations) | printed page xi (PDF page 13)]
Foreword
A troubling paradox is taking shape across the global financing landscape. Access to international finance has improved, but the price of that finance has not. Low- and middle-income countries are borrowing more, paying more, and, in many cases, leaving less for long-term development.
The numbers are striking. In 2025, external debt across low- and middle-income countries surged 5.5 percent to a record $9.4 trillion, the largest annual increase in four years. Private lenders returned, bond markets reopened, and governments found new paths to financing that had been closed off during the preceding years of rate tightening and risk aversion. On the surface, this looks like a recovery. Beneath the headline numbers, however, a more complicated picture emerges.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Front matter (Foreword, Key Takeaways, Abbreviations) | printed page xi (PDF page 13)]
The return to international capital markets has been highly uneven. The poorest and most vulnerable countries face borrowing costs not seen since the late 1980s. Low- and middle-income countries’ total debt service burden rose for a fifth consecutive year in 2025, which means that more public resources are being absorbed by servicing debt at a time when countries need to invest more in infrastructure, jobs, education, health, and the foundations of long-term growth.
Continued borrowing through international bond markets in 2026, despite elevated yields, raises important questions about whether the terms are sustainable and whether the capital raised is reaching the people and places that need it most.
This question has become more urgent in a global economy increasingly prone to shocks. Over the past decade, countries have confronted a pandemic, disruption to trade and supply chains, a sharp increase in food and energy prices, geopolitical fragmentation, and repeated episodes of financial market volatility. Such shocks are difficult for any economy to absorb. It is harder still when governments already face substantial financing needs and limited room to respond.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Front matter (Foreword, Key Takeaways, Abbreviations) | printed page xi (PDF page 13)]
The consequences extend beyond government balance sheets, as debt vulnerabilities are not simply a financial concern. When debt service constrains productive and social spending, the consequences can ultimately reach households through weaker investment, fewer opportunities, and greater vulnerability to shocks. For example, the report finds that, during periods of external shocks,

Against this backdrop, knowing how much countries owe, to whom, and on what terms has never been more important.

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Front matter (Foreword, Key Takeaways, Abbreviations) | printed page xii (PDF page 14)]
For more than five decades, the World Bank Group has worked with borrowing countries to build the most comprehensive source of comparable external debt data for developing economies. But transparency cannot rest on debtor reporting alone. A major advance in recent years has been the systematic reconciliation of loan-by-loan information reported by borrowers through the World Bank Group’s Debtor Reporting System with corresponding records provided by bilateral creditors. The results show what cooperation between borrowers and creditors can achieve. Since the creditor data-sharing exercise began in 2022, successive rounds have helped reconcile loan-level records, identify discrepancies, validate information, and close critical data gaps, strengthening the quality and consistency of external debt statistics. This is debt transparency in practice. It is not simply about publishing more data. It is about comparing borrowers’ and creditors’ records, identifying inconsistencies, resolving differences, and progressively improving the common information base on which debt decisions are made.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Front matter (Foreword, Key Takeaways, Abbreviations) | printed page xii (PDF page 14)]
That work becomes even more important as sovereign financing grows more complex. New creditors, instruments, guarantees, restructurings, and financing arrangements can make it harder to establish a complete picture of a country’s obligations. Without reliable and reconciled information, governments cannot manage debt effectively, creditors cannot assess risks accurately, and debt restructurings can become more difficult.
Transparency is a shared responsibility. Borrowers must maintain comprehensive and timely debt records; creditors, official and private, should disclose the information needed to understand those obligations; and international institutions must strengthen standards, close data gaps, and support stronger debt management systems.
Better information must ultimately lead to better financing. Countries bearing some of the greatest development burdens continue to face some of the steepest borrowing costs, a paradox that compounds their disadvantages at every turn. Financing that merely enables countries to roll over costly debt cannot substitute for financing that expands productive capacity and raises future incomes.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Front matter (Foreword, Key Takeaways, Abbreviations) | printed page xii (PDF page 14)]
The objective should, therefore, not be more debt. It should be better financing that is affordable, transparent, sustainable, and capable of supporting investment and growth.

The message of this year’s report is clear: access to finance is not enough. We must know the debt, understand its terms, and ensure that the financing developing economies receive strengthens rather than constrains their ability to grow, withstand shocks, and improve the lives of their people.

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Front matter (Foreword, Key Takeaways, Abbreviations) | printed page xvii (PDF page 19)]
Key Takeaways
Borrowing by low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) surged in 2025, marking the sharpest increase in external debt in four years and a forceful return of private creditors to developing country markets. External debt climbed to a record $9.4 trillion as bond issues rebounded, the US dollar weakened, and investors again showed greater willingness to lend. But the reopening of capital markets came at a steep price, especially for the poorest countries, which faced some of their highest borrowing costs in decades. Debt service payments also rose for a fifth consecutive year. Even so, stronger economic growth helped stabilize some debt ratios, and net long-term debt transfers turned positive after years of outflows.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Front matter (Foreword, Key Takeaways, Abbreviations) | printed page xvii (PDF page 19)]
• Debt accumulation accelerated sharply in 2025. The external debt of LMICs jumped 5.5 percent to a record $9.4 trillion in 2025, the fastest increase since 2021 and more than four times the average annual growth recorded from 2022 to 2024. The increase in external debt was even faster for countries eligible for International Development Association (IDA) financing, rising 8.1 percent to $1.3 trillion, and for low-income countries, climbing 8.9 percent to $262.4 billion, the biggest increase since 2020.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Front matter (Foreword, Key Takeaways, Abbreviations) | printed page xvii (PDF page 19)]
• A weakening dollar amplified the rise in debt. The dramatic depreciation of the US dollar during the year accounted for 28.2 percent of the increase in LMICs’ external public and publicly guaranteed debt. This outcome reflects an important valuation effect: International Debt Statistics are expressed in US dollars for comparability, including liabilities denominated in other currencies. For several of the largest borrowers from concessional windows, currency valuation gains in 2025 not only offset principal payments made during the year but also, in some cases, partially reversed the stock reductions achieved through repayments in 2024, leaving reported balances higher at end-2025 despite continued debt servicing.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Front matter (Foreword, Key Takeaways, Abbreviations) | printed page xvii (PDF page 19)]
• Private creditors returned to LMICs. Private lending, which is more susceptible to fluctuations in financial market conditions, pricing conditions, and perceived creditworthiness of borrowers, saw a strong rebound in 2025. LMIC debt stock owed to private creditors increased 5.2 percent in 2025 to $5.0 trillion, a significant acceleration from the 0.6 percent increase recorded in 2024. This increase was due to a combined increase in debt owed to bondholders and debt owed to commercial banks and other private
xvii
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Front matter (Foreword, Key Takeaways, Abbreviations) | printed page xviii (PDF page 20)]
creditors, which increased by 5.7 percent (to $2.4 trillion) and 4.7 percent (to $2.7 trillion), respectively. LMIC economies, measured by gross national income, grew by 5.1 percent in 2025. This strong economic growth encouraged lenders to return to these countries, and many LMIC governments were willing to borrow despite relatively high interest rates.
• The countries that can least afford it are paying the most to borrow. Increased borrowing from private creditors hardened lending terms disproportionately for IDA-eligible countries, which faced an average interest rate of 8.2 percent on new commitments during the year, the highest since the late 1980s. The difference in interest rates that this group of borrowers pays when borrowing from official creditors and rates on debt from private creditors widened significantly over the past decade, from 3.4 percentage points in 2016 to 5.5 percentage points in 2025. International Bank for Reconstruction and Development borrowers, by contrast, saw improvements in the terms on new commitments, with an improved 5.5 percent average interest rate, down from 5.8 percent the previous year.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Front matter (Foreword, Key Takeaways, Abbreviations) | printed page xviii (PDF page 20)]
• The bond market reopened for LMICs. After being essentially shut out of international bond markets for several years, LMICs returned to bond markets in force in 2025. Key Takeaways
• Debt burdens eased in IDA-eligible countries but rose elsewhere. Despite a sharp increase in borrowing, IDA-eligible countries saw their external debt burdens decline slightly in 2025. Their debt-to-income ratio fell from 42.1 percent to 41.2 percent, as economic growth outpaced debt accumulation, and some countries benefited from debt restructuring. The picture was different for other developing economies. Excluding China, LMICs saw their debt-to-income ratio rise to 34.5 percent, as debt grew faster than national income.
• Other financial flows to LMICs continue to diverge, with negative consequences. Foreign direct investment (FDI) and personal remittances to LMICs continued to diverge in 2025, a trend that has been accelerating over two decades. LMICs saw their FDI contract by 25.5 percent from 2011 to 2025, whereas remittances more than doubled over the period. In 2025, remittances were about $294.5 billion more than FDI. This growing divide carries long-term implications for growth, because FDI builds productive capacity whereas remittances primarily support households and remain less connected to productive investment.

Renewed global inflationary pressures, geopolitical tensions, and decreased fiscal space continued to put substantial pressure on the external debt positions of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) in 2025. LMICs’ external borrowing levels reached a record $9.4 trillion at the end of the year, increasing 5.5 percent from $8.9 trillion in 2024. LMIC external debt has grown about 60 percent over the past decade, and the 2025 increase was the largest since the easing of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. The change in debt stock was driven by net debt inflows of $423.5 billion, a more than twofold increase from 2024, as well as by some debt forgiveness and the upward accounting effect of US dollar depreciation. During the first half of 2025, the US dollar experienced its biggest depreciation against other currencies in more than five decades, and the increase in new debt flows went largely to middle-income countries (MICs), predominantly because of continued support from multilateral creditors and a rebound in lending from private creditors. That rebound, driven by both new borrowing and buyback operations, indicated a recovery of investor confidence after a retrenchment by private lenders from 2022 to 2023 and only a small increase in 2024, as well as a renewed search for yield (table 1.1). This pattern shows the procyclical nature of the private creditor lending. It expands in favorable global conditions and contracts sharply when conditions tighten. (Refer to box 1.1 for definitions of debt terms used in this report.)

Box 1.2 Total Return Swaps: An Emerging Form of Sovereign Financing
Total return swaps (TRSs) have traditionally been used in financial markets to transfer the economic risks and returns of an underlying asset without transferring its legal ownership. More recently, TRS structures have gained prominence as a form of sovereign financing, often involving up-front funding and the pledging of government securities or other assets as collateral.
How a TRS Works
A TRS is a financial derivative contract in which one party transfers the total economic return of a reference asset, including income and changes in market value, to another party in exchange for a predetermined stream of payments, typically linked to a benchmark interest rate plus a spread.
In sovereign transactions, TRS structures can combine derivative features with financing. This combination can blur the distinction between a financial derivative and conventional borrowing, and makes it important to assess the economic substance of the transaction.
Sovereign borrowers may turn to TRS arrangements when conventional market financing is unavailable, slow, or prohibitively expensive. By using government

The Growing Use of TRSs in Sovereign Financing
Since 2024, TRS arrangements have been identified in Angola, Argentina, Colombia, Nigeria, and Senegal, with financing amounts ranging from about $1.0 billion to $9.3 billion. Maturities have generally ranged from one to three years, and disclosed collateralization ratios have typically been between 133 and 198 percent. Implications for Debt Statistics and Transparency
A TRS is normally a financial derivative, but some structures can also create debt. If the sovereign receives cash up front and is required to repay it regardless of the performance of the underlying assets, the financing creates an unconditional repayment obligation and is therefore recorded as debt. The derivative component is recorded separately. Securities pledged as collateral generally remain on the sovereign’s balance sheet and do not create additional debt simply because they are pledged.

Headline debt statistics may not fully reveal the amount of collateral pledged, exposure to margin calls, or refinancing and liquidity risks. Transparent reporting should therefore provide information on the amount financed, maturity, collateralization ratio and type of collateral, margin requirements, repayment obligations, and rollover or early termination provisions, while separately identifying the financing and derivative components.
External debt, which is usually contracted and denominated in foreign currency, is exposed to year-on-year and intrayear exchange rate fluctuations that affect its rate of accumulation and its debt service payments. Movements in the value of the US dollar against other global currencies affect the value of LMICs’ debt, and the size of these fluctuations in 2025 had important implications for LMICs, particularly those with large dollar-denominated external debt portfolios. For this subset of countries following a flexible exchange rate regime, dollar-denominated debt became cheaper to service.

The effect is particularly pronounced among the concessional arm of all multilateral creditors. SDR-denominated loans represent a significant share of outstanding concessional debt across multilateral institutions, and the dollar’s 5.0 percent depreciation against the SDR in 2025 increased these loans’ dollar- equivalent values correspondingly. Almost three-fourths of total LMIC debt stock owed to bondholders was issued by public sector entities; that share increased 6.2 percent in 2025, to $1.8 trillion. The increase is even more pronounced when China is excluded: debt stock owed to bondholders increased 11.1 percent, to $1.8 trillion, and debt stock owed to commercial banks and other private creditors rose 8.3 percent, to $2.3 trillion (figure 1.3). The increase in private lending, which is highly procyclical, was correlated with this group of countries’ robust economic growth, as measured by their gross national income (GNI), which grew 6.0 percent in 2025. Through the most recent crises, decreases in debt stock from this creditor base have been associated with the 2008 financial crisis, the 2015 turbulence, and the COVID-19 pandemic. Financial support for Ukraine from bilateral and multilateral creditors has reached unprecedented levels since the start of the Ukraine War in February 2022. Official creditors, including the Group of Seven (G-7) bilateral creditors and multilaterals like the European Union and the World Bank Group, provided $122.2 billion in disbursements during the 2022–25 period. This support reshaped the composition of Ukraine’s external debt (figure B1.4.1). Long-term external debt stock rose from $99 billion in 2015 to $227 billion in 2025, but little of that increase was driven by private creditors, whose claims remained broadly flat over the past decade, rising slightly from $72 billion to $82 billion. Debt owed to multilateral creditors accounts for most of the increase. Bilateral claims increased sixfold over the past decade but grew from a much smaller base and remained a modest share of the total. These official creditors delivered support to Ukraine not only through direct lending but also through grants, trust funds, guarantees, and co- and parallel financing, among other financial instruments.

What is unique about this mechanism, compared to direct lending, is that the principal and interest are serviced from future revenues generated by immobilized Russian sovereign assets rather than from Ukraine’s own budget. Those revenues are channeled through the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism, administered by the European Commission. ERA support extended as loans creates a repayment obligation for the government of Ukraine and is therefore recorded as an external debt liability, whereas the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism represents a financial asset of Ukraine available to service the loan. Under the Debtor Reporting System and international statistical standards—the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual, sixth and seventh editions (IMF 2009, 2025) and External Debt Statistics: Guide for Compilers and Users (IMF 2014)— this loan is classified as a debt instrument based on the existence of a contractual obligation to repay principal and/or interest, rather than on the expected source of repayment. Accordingly, borrowing remains a debt liability even when debt service is expected to be financed from proceeds of immobilized or seized assets. Those proceeds provide the mechanism for repayment but do not change the nature of the liability. Only where repayment is legally limited to those proceeds and the borrower has no obligation to cover any shortfall would the arrangement require different statistical treatment.

Net debt inflows (disbursements minus principal repayments) to LMICs grew for a third consecutive year, more than doubling in 2025 to $423.5 billion. From a maturity standpoint, short-term net debt inflows recorded a more than fivefold increase in 2025, to $89.4 billion, and long-term net debt inflows doubled, to $334.1 billion, approximately 78.9 percent of the total volume of net inflows. This increase in long-term net debt inflows was due to the return to lending to LMICs by private creditors in 2025; these creditors accounted for 75.2 percent of the total long-term component and increased their lending volume by 180.5 percent to $251.1 billion. Private net debt flows are highly procyclical in nature, and the return of private investors has been highly correlated with LMICs’ ongoing economic growth since the COVID-19 downturn in 2020. In 2025, LMIC economies, as measured by their GNI, grew 5.1 percent, to a cumulative $40.2 trillion.

When China, which has recorded four consecutive years of net debt outflows, is excluded, LMICs’ net debt inflows increased to a record $527.6 billion in 2025 (figure 1.4). The yearly increase is more than twice the 2024 total volume and is due to record-high net debt inflows from private creditors, which accounted for 80.8 percent of long-term inflows. This group of countries’ net debt inflows from private creditors more than tripled in 2025, to $358.3 billion, with lending from both bondholders and commercial banks recording nearly threefold increases of $177.0 billion and $181.4 billion, respectively. PNG and PPG sector borrowers held an equal share of the volume of these inflows, but obligations to bondholders and commercial banks differed. Net debt inflows to public sector entities from bondholders accounted for 76.6 percent of inflows received from private creditors, at $137.7 billion in 2025, more than twice the volume recorded in the prior year. Although holding a much smaller share, inflows from commercial banks and other private creditors to public sector entities increased at the same rate as bondholders, reaching $42.1 billion in 2025. The opposite is recorded for PNG net debt inflows, where inflows from bondholders stood for a 22.0 percent share (at $39.2 billion) of the total, and banks and other private creditors accounted for a 78.0 percent share (at $139.3 billion). The increase in private creditors’ net debt flows was driven by an increase in new disbursements accompanied by a slowdown in principal repayments over the same period. New disbursements from private creditors lending to the public sector increased 12.1 percent to $367.8 billion, whereas principal repayments decreased by 3.3 percent to $227.3 billion in 2025. Bond issuances accounted for 68.1 percent of these new disbursements, increasing 34.6 percent to $250.6 billion, to volumes not seen since 2021. Notably, when China is excluded, the $238.9 billion issuance is a record for LMICs, reflecting a robust return of investor confidence. The monetary tightening in advanced economies disproportionately affected the riskiest borrowers, and subsequent monetary easing helped improve market conditions and lower borrowing costs from their 2023 peaks. The rebound was substantial both in pace and scale. The increase in new public sector disbursements was driven by Mexico, which accounted for a 16.7 percent share of new LMIC issues, at $42.0 billion in 2025. Türkiye and Colombia were the next largest LMIC public sector issuers, at $27.7 billion and $27.5 billion respectively, which reflects strong international investor demand in 2025.

The headline issuance figure masks a divergence of the use of the proceeds from these international bond sales, however. Some of the proceeds from new debt issuances in 2025 were strategically used to fund LMICs’ ongoing and proactive liability management strategies and operations, particularly debt buyback operations. Fourteen countries carried out such operations to prepay and mature $34.5 billion of their outstanding external debt obligations. The debt management strategies included the use of proceeds from the issuance of new bonds to mature existing liabilities and were part of larger operations, in efforts to alter the maturity structure of these countries’ debt portfolios, to change the currency in which the debt is denominated in order to reduce exchange rate exposure, or to lower the interest rates being charged. Bullet payments of bond obligations coming due over the 2024–26 redemption wall were pushed further into the future through these operations, easing rollover risk pressures.

[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 1. Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025 | printed page 22 (PDF page 46)]
LMICs’ long-term net debt transfers (disbursement minus total debt service payments) turned positive in 2025 after three consecutive years of negative volumes. Negative net transfers were recorded since 2022, during the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, indicating that LMICs’ new disbursements were lower than what they paid in interest and principal payments to service their debt obligations. In 2025, net debt transfers on long-term debt turned positive, reversing from an outflow of $118.4 billion in 2024 to an inflow of $45.4 billion (figure 1.7). The improvement was due to net transfers to PPG borrowers, which increased more than sevenfold to $49.9 billion, after turning slightly positive in 2024 to $6.6 billion. Conversely, net debt transfers to PNG borrowers continued to remain negative in 2025, albeit at an improving pace. Net transfers to PNG borrowers remained negative for the fourth consecutive year but improved considerably, from an outflow of $125.0 billion in 2024 to an outflow of $4.5 billion in 2025. The substantial rise in new gross financing of 17.3 percent, combined with a much slower increase of 2.3 percent in debt service payments, resulted in the improvement in long-term net transfers to LMICs in 2025. This change is even more pronounced when China is excluded. Net transfers on long- term debt to LMICs excluding China reversed from an outflow of $48.5 billion to an inflow of $200.5 billion. For this group of countries, new gross financing increased at a much faster pace in 2025, at 25.2 percent to $1.1 trillion, and long-term debt service payments decreased by 2.4 percent, to $923.8 billion.

Increased borrowing from private creditors has affected country lending groups disproportionately and has led to a hardening of the average terms of new loan commitments to IDA-eligible countries. These countries continued to face ever- increasing average interest rates on their new commitments, with rates reaching 8.2 percent in 2025, up 0.6 percentage point (figure 1.10). Such high average rates have not been seen since 1989 for this group of countries and pose a challenge for their economic development. [International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 1. Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025 | printed page 27 (PDF page 51)]
As IDA-eligible countries continued to tap international markets to issue new bonds, they needed to pay even higher interest rates to attract investors to these instruments. Average interest rates on external commitments of IDA-eligible countries to bondholders increased 1.0 percentage point in 2025 to 9.4 percent, and remained above rates of IBRD borrowers, which experienced a decrease of 0.3 percentage point to 5.5 percent (figure 1.11). The return of international investors to IDA- eligible countries remains uneven, concentrated in the largest borrowers, and costly, as international investors have increased their search for yield. IDA borrowers have therefore absorbed global financial shocks disproportionately. The recovery of IDA- eligible countries’ issuance at yields above 8 percent implies materially higher rollover costs and could place further pressure on interest-to-revenue ratios and financing needs. For many frontier issuers, the binding constraint has consequently shifted from market access to market affordability.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

Box 1.5  Early 2026 Data Show No Signs of Slowdown in LMIC Bond Market Activity
Preliminary data on public and publicly guaranteed (PPG) bond issuances for the first seven and a half months of 2026 show no signs of a slowdown in the appetite of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) for external capital market financing. In fact, more than 10 countries had already surpassed their full-year 2025 PPG bond totals before 2026 reached its midpoint, and the share of bond issuances with maturities of 10 years or more rose as well.
The breadth of market access expanded notably in the first months of 2026. Several countries accessed international bond markets as PPG issuers without having done so at all in 2025. For example, the Democratic Republic of Congo issued $1.25 billion across two bonds at coupons of 8.75 and 9.50 percent, among the highest sovereign coupon rates recorded in 2026 so far.

[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 1. Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025 | printed page 29 (PDF page 53)]
For several countries, issuance volumes through mid-August 2026 already exceeded their full-year 2025 totals. Angola issued $4.75 billion through mid- August 2026, more than double the $2.01 billion issued across all of 2025. Its weighted average coupon also rose to 9.6 percent, up from 8.6 percent in 2025. Bosnia and Herzegovina raised $1.8 billion through mid-August, versus $412 million for all of 2025. India more than doubled its full-year 2025 PPG bond total of $1.0 billion by mid-August 2026, raising $2.5 billion. Indonesia and the Philippines also surpassed their respective 2025 full-year totals.
Borrowing costs for the most vulnerable economies remained elevated and, in several cases, rose further. For Sub-Saharan African issuers specifically, the weighted average coupon on PPG bonds rose from 8.0 percent in 2025 to 8.8 percent through mid-August 2026, and the average maturity on new Sub- Saharan African PPG bonds shortened from 10.4 years in 2025 to 8.9 years, a simultaneous deterioration in both the cost and the tenor of market access.

Across the broader LMIC universe, maturities lengthened compared with 2025, reflecting a shift toward longer-tenor issuances among major borrowers. Bonds with maturities of 10 years or more accounted for 41.5 percent of total PPG issuance volume through mid-August 2026, up from 36.1 percent across all of 2025. Several major issuers, including Brazil, Mexico, and Türkiye, issued across multiple maturity tranches in a single transaction, a structure that allows borrowers to simultaneously refinance near-term obligations and extend their debt profiles.
This maturity extension has unfolded against a backdrop of elevated global borrowing costs. Through mid-2026, benchmark government bond yields in major advanced economies reached multiyear highs, reflecting persistent inflationary pressures, rising public debt issuance volumes across advanced economies, and a prolonged period of restrictive monetary policy. Taken together, early 2026 PPG bond data suggest that LMIC governments have maintained robust access to international capital markets, even as the cost of that access, particularly for lower-income and frontier borrowers, has climbed. The expansion in the number of countries issuing, the pace of issuance relative to 2025, and maturities for select countries all point to continued, if increasingly expensive, engagement with private creditors. External debt flows should be considered alongside other cross-border financing flows that shape the resources available to LMICs. Aggregate financial inflows, comprising debt and equity flows, provide an important measure of cross-border financial integration. 1. Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025
Key Debt Indicators, 2015–25
In 2025, LMICs’ external debt ratios remained mainly stable from the peak levels recorded during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020; however, aggregate improvement was uneven, with debt stock ratios rising or holding flat while debt service and interest payment ratios declined across most borrower groups. This change in ratios reflects a combination of strong export and income growth, the completion of debt restructuring agreements in several IDA-eligible countries, and the depreciation of the US dollar, which inflated the dollar-measured value of both debt stocks and GNI simultaneously through an accounting effect, partly moderating ratio movements in both directions. Ratios of debt to national income and exports are valuable indicators of countries’ ability to service their debt.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 1. Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025 | printed page 35 (PDF page 59)]
For LMICs excluding China, the external debt-to-GNI ratio increased from 33.5 percent in 2024 to 34.5 percent in 2025, as the rise in debt stock of 9.1 percent exceeded GNI growth of 6.0 percent in 2025. The external debt stock of the group reached $7.2 trillion in 2025, an increase of 56.4 percent compared to 2015, reflecting a decade of external borrowing that has increased the debt burden in absolute terms. LMICs excluding China improved in the overall debt service-to-GNI ratio, from 5.1 percent in 2024 to 4.7 percent in 2025, with total debt service declining from $1 trillion to $979 billion. Moreover, interest payments also declined modestly, with the interest payment-to-GNI ratio declining from 1.5 in 2024 to 1.4 percent in 2025.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 1. Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025 | printed page 35 (PDF page 59)]
The external debt-to-GNI ratio in IDA-eligible countries declined from 42.1 percent in 2024 to 41.2 percent in 2025, an improvement after two consecutive years of increases that took the ratio from 30.5 percent in 2015 to its peak in 2024 (figure 1.16). This improvement was driven by GNI growth of 10.5 percent that outpaced the 8.1 percent increase in debt stock. The debt service-to-GNI and interest-to-GNI ratios for IDA-eligible countries declined from 4.2 percent and 1.4 percent in 2024 to 3.7 percent and 1.3 percent, respectively, in 2025, reflecting a 2.3 percent decrease in total debt service obligations and stable interest payments. Similarly, LICs recorded a marginal deterioration in their external debt-to-GNI ratio, which rose from 41.1 percent in 2024 to 42.3 percent in 2025, as debt stock growth outpaced income growth; the debt service-to-GNI ratio remained broadly stable at approximately 2.0 percent in both years. The interest-to-GNI ratio also improved slightly, from 1.1 percent in 2024 to 1.0 percent in 2025, supported by income growth outpacing flat interest payments of $6.0 billion. Yet interest costs for this group have grown at nearly double the annual average rate recorded over the 2015–25 period, reflecting the structural rise in borrowing costs in recent years.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 1. Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025 | printed page 36 (PDF page 60)]
The 2025 data point to a range of outcomes for the group and regions, with a few recording distinct trends. Sub-Saharan Africa continued to carry one of the heaviest debt burdens relative to income, with the debt-to-GNI ratio at 48.0 percent, well above the 34.4 percent recorded in 2015 and equivalent to nearly half of the region’s annual national income. Debt service and interest payments relative to GNI, at 4.4 and 1.6 percent, respectively, remained among the highest recorded for the region over the decade, but both ratios are partly weighted by South Africa’s contribution to the regional aggregate. Europe and Central Asia retained the highest debt service-to-GNI and interest-to-GNI ratios among all LMIC regions in 2025, at 7.9 and 2.2 percent respectively; however, the debt service-to-GNI ratio declined slightly from 8.1 percent in 2024, and the interest-to-GNI ratio remained stable. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan region recorded the largest single-year increase in its debt-to-GNI ratio of any region, rising from 26.7 to 29.4 percent, signaling continued stock accumulation even as its debt service ratios improved by 0.4 percentage point in 2025 to 3.1 percent.

Trends in External Debt of IDA-Eligible Countries, 2015–25
External debt stock of IDA-eligible countries reached a record $1.3 trillion in 2025, accumulating at a rate of 8.1 percent, faster than that of the other LMICs. The pace of accumulation was much higher than the 2.9 percent average recorded during the past three years and raises sustainability concerns for this group of countries. Long-term debt stock rose by 7.9 percent, and short-term debt rose by 10.7 percent, bringing the end-2025 external debt stock to almost double the 2015 level. Long-term obligations of the PPG sector grew at a faster rate of 9.0 percent than the 4.3 percent increase of the PNG debt stock. The restoration of access to capital markets has been particularly consequential for Sub-Saharan Africa, which accounted for 64 percent of IDA-eligible countries’ total public sector issuances (figure 1.19). The public sectors of eight countries in Sub-Saharan Africa collectively raised approximately $11.8 billion by end-December 2025, a marked 36.2 percent increase over 2024. Several issuers returned after prolonged absences: Kenya, the largest issuer in the region, raised $3.5 billion in 2025. The country returned to bond markets to prepay its 2027 and 2028 maturity obligations ahead of schedule. Côte d’Ivoire raised a total of $2.5 billion in 2025. Importantly, a substantial share of proceeds from the two countries’ debt offerings funded their liability management operations, refinancing upcoming bullet maturities, and thereby easing rollover pressures. Nigeria, the third-largest issuer in the region, raised $2.3 billion in a dual-tranche international bond issue that was divided into one tranche with a 10-year maturity at 8.625 percent and a second, 20-year maturity tranche at 9.125 percent. Remarkably, Uganda’s share of domestic currency government debt held by nonresidents reached $2.8 billion in 2025, indicating strong demand for high-yield debt from international investors. Among countries in other regions, Uzbekistan recorded the highest international bond issuance among IDA-eligible countries in 2025, at $3.9 billion. The public sector issuance was divided between $1.6 billion in issuances from the general government sector, including issuances in domestic currency, and $2.4 billion in issuances from other public sector entities. Suriname completed its first international issuance since 2016.

After hitting an all-time high in 2024, the cost of servicing IDA-eligible countries’ external debt obligations (interest plus principal repayments) decreased 2.3 percent in 2025, to $117.2 billion. The decrease in total debt servicing cost was due to a 2.9 percent decrease in principal repayments on total external debt, to $77.6 billion, which accounted for a 66 percent share of the total payments made by this group of countries in 2025. Interest payments on total liabilities also decreased, by 1.2 percent, to $39.6 billion in 2025, after recording a record high volume of $40.1 billion in 2024. From a debtor’s viewpoint, the decrease was led by PNG sector borrowing, which fell 9.5 percent to $40.9 billion, but the cost of servicing public sector debt continued to increase, by 2.5 percent, in 2025 to $71.3 billion. Debt service payments on PPG debt have been on the rise for five consecutive years since 2020 and marked another record high for IDA- eligible countries in 2025. The increase continues to limit these countries’ fiscal space and raises sustainability concerns for this group, which is eligible to borrow on concessional terms from IDA to support countries’ debt sustainability and includes some of the poorest countries.

Debt service payments from PPG borrowers to multilateral institutions and private creditors were the main drivers of the increase in total PPG debt service costs. Debt service payments to multilateral institutions increased 3.6 percent, to $30.6 billion, and accounted for 42.9 percent of PPG borrowers’ total payments. IDA-eligible countries owe more than half of their public sector debt to this group of creditors because of the concessional terms these institutions typically provide. Notably, as principal payments made to this creditor base increased 7.6 percent in 2025, to $20.3 billion, interest payments decreased 3.5 percent to $10.3 billion. Debt service payments made by public sector entities to bondholders increased at a much faster pace of 16.9 percent, to $13.1 billion. Bondholders accounted for 18.4 percent of the debt service payments to PPG creditors, an increase of 8 percentage points since 2023. This share has been increasing over the past two years, whereas the respective share in debt stock position has remained stable over the decade at an average of 12 percent. Principal repayments made to this creditor group increased 5.8 percent in 2025, to $6.6 billion, and included advance repayments from buyback operations made by Kenya and Suriname. Interest payments increased at a much faster pace of 30.7 percent in 2025, to $6.5 billion. These costs are projected to increase as IDA-eligible countries continue to tap international markets at an accelerated pace, amid an environment of elevated global interest rates.

Efforts to enhance the debt restructuring architecture continued in 2025 primarily through reforms to the G-20 Common Framework, facilitated by the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable. Since its creation in 2020, the G-20 Common Framework has served as the coordinating mechanism for the provision of comprehensive debt restructuring for IDA-eligible countries. It brings together all G-20 bilateral creditors and coordinates with private creditor groups to provide a debt treatment, tailored to each borrower’s debt structure, to restore medium-term debt sustainability. A key area of progress in 2025 was the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable endorsement of early publication by the debtor of the key debt restructuring parameters, namely (a) the net present value reduction; (b) the reduction in debt service over the IMF program period; and (c) the change in the duration of treated claims. This information provides private creditors with an up-front indicator of comparability of treatment requirements.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

Liability Management Operations in 2025 Tenders by LMICs to buy back or exchange sovereign bonds increased markedly in 2025 as governments used new bond issuance to refinance existing obligations and actively manage their debt portfolios. Based on data reported to the Debtor Reporting System, 14 countries repurchased $34.5 billion in outstanding sovereign bonds in 2025, with the largest operations concentrated in MICs (figure 1.22). Although the scale and structure of these transactions varied, both middle-income and IDA-eligible countries sought to reduce near-term refinancing pressures, extend maturity profiles, manage currency and interest rate exposure, and, in some cases, support state-owned enterprises. [International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 51 (PDF page 75)]
External Debt, External Shocks, and Vulnerability in LMICs
Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are facing historically high global uncertainty at a time when external debt stocks have reached historic highs, debt service pressures remain elevated, fiscal space is limited in many countries, and global bond yields continue to rise, tightening financial conditions. This combination matters because external shocks can be more difficult to absorb when governments already face substantial financing needs and limited room to respond. The key vulnerability therefore lies not in exposure to global shocks alone but in how those shocks interact with already-high debt burdens. Adverse developments in trade, commodity markets, growth, exchange rates, and tighter global financing conditions all have the potential to weaken external and fiscal positions, and high debt levels can amplify their economic and development consequences and impair the effectiveness of policy responses.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 51 (PDF page 75)]
International Debt Report 2025 documented the scale of external debt burdens and their links to economic growth and vulnerability (World Bank 2025). Building on that assessment, this year’s report focuses on the interactions between external shocks and external debt burdens, and how debt might amplify vulnerabilities when global conditions deteriorate. This chapter examines the channels through which these interactions operate across LMICs. The chapter further discusses how rising debt service burdens, elevated financing needs, and changing financing patterns are constraining fiscal space and intensifying debt and rollover risks, as well as the policy priorities for strengthening resilience. Finally, food and nutrition security provides a concrete example of these interactions, illustrating how debt burdens may be closely associated with a decline in the affordability of a healthy diet during periods of global stress.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 51 (PDF page 75)]
Global uncertainty rose sharply in 2025 (figure 2.1) and remained elevated into 2026. The World Uncertainty Index measures broad uncertainty and rose more than fivefold between the third quarter of 2024 and the third quarter of 2025, nearly twice its COVID-19 peak. The Global Economic Policy Uncertainty Index showed a similar pattern, rising sharply in early 2025 and remaining elevated into 2026 (Ahir et al. 2022; Davis 2016).1
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 52 (PDF page 76)]
Elevated uncertainty matters because economies remain closely connected to international markets. Yet countries differ in the nature and degree of their external exposure, which shapes how global external shocks affect them. Trade provides an important example. As figure 2.2 shows, global imports and exports of goods and services increased from below 25 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the early 2000s, were halted by the 2008 global financial crisis, and subsequently rebounded and have fluctuated around 30 percent. Exposure, however, varies significantly across income groups. In 2025, imports accounted for about 34 percent of GDP in low-income economies, compared with exports of about 24 percent; trade flows were much more balanced in high-income economies.
The next section discusses these transmission channels in greater detail, including the roles of trade and financial exposure, exchange rates, inflation, and policy buffers, and how external debt can amplify vulnerabilities when shocks occur.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 53 (PDF page 77)]
External shocks are transmitted to LMICs differently, depending on their structural features. Economies that rely heavily on imports of goods and services for domestic activity are vulnerable to sudden changes in the external environment, such as production shortfalls in major supplier countries, export restrictions, or supply chain disruptions; in contrast, export-oriented economies are more vulnerable to shifts in demand among their trading partners. External shocks also tend to spill more forcefully into LMICs with open financial markets, partly reflecting rapid capital flow movements. In addition, the types of policy frameworks in LMICs are important for the transmission of external shocks. For example, in economies with flexible exchange rate regimes, the effects of external shocks are partly absorbed through currency movements. In economies with fixed exchange rate regimes, pressure on the exchange rate can be cushioned by using foreign reserves. As discussed later in this chapter, damage from external shocks that LMICs can absorb and the speed of subsequent recovery are also subject to the availability of fiscal buffers and the implementation of fiscal and foreign exchange policy frameworks.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

External debt is a key amplifier of the transmission of external shocks. Economies with elevated external debt levels, especially short-term debt, are vulnerable to sudden shifts in investor risk appetite and rollover risks, potentially leading to sudden stops in capital flows and current account reversals. For most LMICs, where external debt tends to be denominated in foreign currencies, economic vulnerabilities can increase when external shocks lead to currency depreciation, causing an increase in debt service burdens and higher inflation. An increase in debt service costs can slow investment growth by decreasing national savings. During periods of tightening global financial conditions, LMICs with high levels of external debt need to raise interest rates to defend their currencies, causing credit crunches in domestic financial markets and slowing growth.

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 55 (PDF page 79)]
The nature of external shocks also affects the different degrees of shock transmission to LMICs. For example, global supply shocks, including shortages of energy, food, and other commodities—and rapid increases in their prices, which tend to be caused by wars and conflicts as well as extreme weather- related events—have a larger impact on commodity importers. The outbreak of a conflict involving major commodity producers can halt their exports, and the impact can be exacerbated by logistical disruptions such as port or shipping lane closures. Particularly in food-producing economies, disasters associated with extreme weather, including storms and droughts potentially caused by El Niño, can decrease global food production and disrupt global trade. In addition, abrupt shifts in trade policies, including the imposition of tariffs or export bans, can restrict access to key commodities. In contrast, commodity exporters tend to be affected more by adverse global demand shocks, including slowdowns in global activity triggered by major systemic events such as financial crises and pandemic-driven lockdowns, and the resulting plunges in commodity prices.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 55 (PDF page 79)]
In commodity-importing LMICs, external shocks can be transmitted through multiple channels. Higher global energy and food prices, along with disruptions to shipping and global value chains, raise production and transportation costs. The resulting rise in domestic inflation in these economies drives up the cost of living, with disproportionate effects on poorer economies and households, where food accounts for a larger share of consumption. The purchasing power of consumers declines as real incomes fall, resulting in reduced spending. In addition, higher prices of commodities and other imported materials increase overall import costs, worsening terms of trade and current account balances. Financial conditions can tighten because of hikes in interest rates to combat increased inflation, raising borrowing costs. Pressures of currency depreciation rise, increasing the costs of servicing debt denominated in foreign currencies. Fiscal positions deteriorate, with increasing spending pressures, including fuel and food subsidies, and slower activity can lower revenue collection.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 56 (PDF page 80)]
Inflation in commodity-importing LMICs has increased following a major energy supply shock in 2026. The conflict in the Middle East involving major energy producers, which began at the end of February 2026, has caused a surge in headline inflation in these countries, to 3.6 percent in June 2026, from the preconflict level of 2.6 percent (figure 2.4). Among market participants, inflation expectations for 2026 have also risen, from 2.7 percent according to preconflict February surveys to 3.4 percent in July. Excluding China, which has been relatively insulated from the shock, partly because of its large petroleum reserves, inflation in commodity-importing LMICs increased from 7.0 percent to 8.3 percent between January and June, with higher inflation expectations for 2026. Energy prices have increased, as well, by 1.1 percentage points between January and June 2026 (excluding China). To ease price pressures, several central banks have raised interest rates. In addition, several commodity- importing LMICs have introduced subsidies in response to higher fuel prices (World Bank 2026b).
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

The energy supply shock in 2026 has caused exchange rates in commodity- importing LMICs to fall, worsening trade balances. Among commodity-importing LMICs with flexible or adjustable exchange rate regimes, currencies depreciated by about 1.7 percent between January and July 2026 (figure 2.5), on average. In contrast, currencies in commodity-exporting LMICs with flexible regimes appreciated by an average of 2.5 percent over the same period. Currency pressures have made imports more expensive in commodity importers and worsened trade balances. Across commodity-importing LMICs with flexible or adjustable currency regimes, merchandise import values, in US dollar terms, increased by an average 23 percent between February and June 2026 compared with the same months of 2025. Excluding China, the rate of increase was 21 percent, on average. As import values increased faster than those of exports, merchandise trade deficits—without China—expanded in the first half of 2026. Between February and June 2026, merchandise trade deficits averaged almost $20 billion higher than in the same months of the previous year.

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 58 (PDF page 82)]
Global demand shocks affect commodity-exporting LMICs directly and indirectly. Collapses in global commodity prices directly reduce export earnings and profits in the commodity-related sector, reducing domestic demand and activity. Revenue declines cause deterioration of fiscal positions and the debt service mechanism, while also leading to worsening terms of trade and current account balances. With reduced debt repayment capacity, sovereign risk premiums increase, raising debt refinancing costs, eroding investor confidence, and potentially triggering sudden capital outflows. Financial conditions are tightened, with lower credit availability and a weakened banking sector, along with a rise in nonperforming loans. Declines in foreign exchange earnings also lead to currency depreciation, which increases inflationary pressure and living costs.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 58 (PDF page 82)]
The impact of external shocks tends to be larger and more persistent in fragile economies and low-income countries (LICs). In both LICs and economies in fragile, conflict, and violence-affected environments or with institutional fragility, financial markets tend to be shallower than in other LMICs, making them more exposed to external shocks. They tend to rely on narrower economic bases, in terms of exports and revenue sources, and are therefore more affected by sudden shifts in external conditions. With a weak institutional framework and limited access to financing, these economies tend to implement procyclical fiscal tightening during economic downturns. Increases in commodity prices and supply shortages translate into substantial losses in economic welfare and income, reflecting persistently low personal savings and acute food insecurity.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 58 (PDF page 82)]
International reserves and credible monetary policies can help cushion the adverse impact of external shocks in LMICs. The accumulation of foreign exchange reserves can defend against sharp currency depreciation and can be used to pay for imports of commodities and other essential products. LMICs have increased their foreign exchange reserves over the past decade, reaching more than $6 trillion at the end of June 2026. Excluding China, foreign exchange increased to $2.6 trillion in June. However, the pace of foreign exchange accumulation has slowed since March 2026, particularly in commodity-importing LMICs, mainly because of the conflict in the Middle East (figure 2.6). Facing a rise in import costs driven by currency depreciation, some of these economies have been forced to draw on their reserves. This trend has been exacerbated by outflows of foreign currency, mainly driven by rising global risk aversion. In addition, credible monetary policy frameworks act as critical policy buffers against external shocks in LMICs. They help anchor long-term inflation expectations and reduce the transmission of global shocks, such as commodity price changes and financial market volatility, to domestic inflation. Preconditions for the effectiveness of the frameworks include greater independence for central banks and transparent communication of monetary policy.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 59 (PDF page 83)]
Robust fiscal policy frameworks can also act as strong policy buffers against external shocks. Fiscal rules help manage revenue volatility and excess spending during booms; stabilization funds, especially in commodity-exporting LMICs, can mitigate the procyclicality of fiscal policy by saving revenues during booms and deploying them when commodity prices and revenues collapse. Since 2000, many commodity-exporting LMICs have adopted such frameworks (figure 2.7). However, successful implementation requires strong institutions, including transparency and technical capacity (Vasishtha 2026). Policy priorities differ across LMICs, depending on the strength of institutional capacity and fiscal space. Economies with weaker capacity need to strengthen tax revenue mobilization and improve fiscal transparency.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

Debt Sustainability and Fiscal Pressures
External shocks have compounded preexisting fiscal pressures and increased debt vulnerabilities in LMICs. These countries require substantial investment to raise productivity, create jobs, and advance broader development objectives. Financing these needs depends on mobilizing domestic resources, attracting domestic and foreign private capital, and, where necessary, borrowing through public channels. In this context, part of the increase in public debt reflects efforts to finance infrastructure, human capital, and other investments that can support long-term growth. However, slower global growth, policy uncertainty, trade fragmentation, geopolitical tensions, and commodity-price volatility have affected both the availability and cost of financing. In many countries, shocks that initially generated temporary financing needs have contributed to persistently higher debt stocks, debt service burdens, and rollover requirements.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

Sovereign credit rating actions remained in flux throughout 2025. For instance, in the first half of 2025, Fitch recorded eight sovereign upgrades against four downgrades among emerging markets—a net positive trend—but revised its sector outlook for Asia-Pacific, Eastern Europe, and Sub-Saharan Africa to “deteriorating” from “neutral,” citing trade uncertainty and tightening fiscal space. Moody’s downgraded Bolivia and Botswana, while upgrading Costa Rica. This mixed picture illustrates that sovereign creditworthiness is increasingly differentiated and that the gap between countries that gain and lose market confidence is often shaped not only by fundamentals but also by how effectively governments engage with investors and creditors.

Against this backdrop, the World Bank Group has published “Sovereign Investor Relations: A Guide for Debt Managers” (Proite and Yavuz 2026), a practical handbook designed to help debt managers in low- and middle-income countries build and professionalize their investor relations functions. The guide argues that countries must move from passive disclosure to active, structured engagement that reduces information asymmetries to lower the “uncertainty premium” embedded in their borrowing costs. The guidance note covers the full spectrum of sovereign investor relations, from strategy formulation to institutional setup as well as practical tools for implementation. The guide is scalable and designed for countries at varying stages of market development, from frontier markets taking their first steps in external borrowing to frequent issuers seeking to deepen and diversify their investor bases.

Countries that engage creditors early, communicate policy intent clearly, and manage reputational risk systematically are better positioned to preserve market access, reduce financing costs, and navigate periods of stress.

[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 63 (PDF page 87)]
The persistence of high GFNs, despite narrower primary deficits, underscores the role of accumulated debt and higher debt service costs. Notwithstanding notable fiscal consolidation, with primary deficits in 2023–24 narrowing to approximately half their 2021–22 levels, average GFNs stabilized at about 8 percent of GDP, 2 percentage points above their prepandemic average, before increasing further in 2025. Consistent with this pattern, the distribution of debt-stabilization gaps across countries has changed little over the past 15 years (figure 2.9). These gaps, denoted as ΔDSPD, are calculated as the difference between the actual primary deficit and the debt-stabilizing primary deficit, indicating the primary deficit or surplus that would keep the debt-to-GDP ratio unchanged, given the country’s existing debt, borrowing costs, and GDP growth.2 This calculation suggests that the continued elevation of GFNs is not primarily the result of a renewed widening of primary deficits. Rather, it reflects the debt stock accumulated following successive shocks, higher interest costs, the rollover of maturing obligations, and, in some cases, balance of payments financing needs.

Debt distress risks have eased from the deterioration observed over the past decade, particularly following the COVID-19 shock, but they remain elevated. Box 2.2  Strengthening the Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries
The 2026 review of the Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries by the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group updates how the organizations assess sovereign debt risk and sustainability amid rising domestic borrowing, diversified creditor bases, and growing liquidity pressures. The revisions aim to strengthen early warning capacity and policy relevance while preserving the framework’s role in guiding borrowing and lending decisions. Key reforms include the following:
•	 A revamped risk architecture distinguishing more clearly between external debt stress, overall public debt stress, and unsustainability
•	 The introduction of new models for the risk of overall public debt stress and public debt unsustainability, together with an updated model for the risk of external public debt stress
•	 New dedicated modules to support the structured application of judgment, including
– A domestic debt module to assess solvency, liquidity risk, and macro­ financial linkages (including the sovereign–bank–central bank nexus); and
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 65 (PDF page 89)]
– A long-term module to evaluate implications of policy and investment deci­ sions (including climate adaptation, infrastructure, and human capital) over longer horizons
•	 New emphasis on data quality via the new debt data confidence flag, clearer guidance on the debt perimeter, and incentives to close reporting gaps
•	 Introduction of additional granularity to risk ratings to differentiate among countries at high risk of debt distress.
The review was launched in 2024 with public consultations and stakeholder inputs gathered through 2026. The new framework is expected to become operational in the second half of 2027, allowing time to finalize the revised operational guidance and undertake extensive capacity building for users of the framework.

Domestic creditors in both IDA and International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) countries have elevated their exposure to the sovereign over the past 20 years. This move mirrors their respective governments’ growing reliance on domestic financing. However, domestic banks in IDA countries have consistently held a greater share of their balance sheets in sovereign assets than banks in IBRD countries have (figure 2.11). This higher exposure reflects less developed and less diversified private sectors in many IDA countries, as well as fewer investment options as compared to IBRD markets. Domestic banks may therefore have few alternatives to government securities, particularly during periods of financial stress. In IDA countries, the increase in sovereign exposure goes beyond the domestic banking sector to include the central bank and the domestic nonbanking sector (figure 2.12).

borrowing increases exposure to exchange rate and refinancing shocks. At the same time, high debt limits countries’ ability to borrow to close financing gaps. Countries are therefore left increasingly exposed to shocks, with minimal fiscal and financial buffers.
Sound fiscal and debt policies are central to preparing for, responding to, and recovering from external shocks. Fiscal buffers and debt sustainability determine the extent to which countries can absorb shocks and support recovery. Countries that entered shock episodes with adequate fiscal buffers, manageable debt levels, and a track record of countercyclical policies consistently limited long- term output losses. By contrast, high debt and procyclical spending amplified the economic damage.4 The interaction of limited fiscal buffers, elevated debt vulnerabilities, and weak policy execution points to three interconnected priorities: revenue mobilization and maintaining sound debt management, adopting countercyclical fiscal strategies, and investing in fiscal institutions.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 68 (PDF page 92)]
Mobilizing revenue and managing debt. Revenue mobilization is not simply a matter of raising tax rates. Effective mobilization requires a holistic approach that strengthens the policy, administrative, and legal foundations of the tax system in tandem (Benitez et al. 2023). Without this broader institutional underpinning, additional revenue efforts risk being partial, inequitable, or unsustainable, undermining the fiscal resilience they are intended to build.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 68 (PDF page 92)]
Effective debt management requires not only controlling the overall level of debt but also managing its composition and risk profile, including maturity, currency, interest rate, refinancing, and creditor risks. Sound debt management acts as a key shock absorber during times of crisis. Poor borrowing choices made during periods of stress can worsen liquidity and solvency risks, particularly when governments turn to short-term solutions that are less transparent or less market based, such as private placements or collateralized borrowing. These instruments may provide immediate financing, but they can also increase rollover risks, reduce transparency, constrain future policy choices, and expose public assets or future revenues to claims. Governments should therefore design, implement, and communicate contingent borrowing plans before crises occur.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 68 (PDF page 92)]
Conducting fiscal policy over the economic cycle. Economies that ran procyclical spending policies and persistent deficits over time faced economically larger and longer-lasting output losses from external shocks, whereas those that maintained countercyclical spending and ran primary surpluses, on average, experienced little to no losses. Dependence on commodities for exports and fiscal revenues makes commodity- exporting LMICs particularly exposed to swings in commodity prices.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 69 (PDF page 93)]
During commodity price booms and the resulting rise in fiscal revenues, governments in those economies tend to increase spending. Without primary surpluses, those economies tend to have fewer fiscal resources to support activity and protect vulnerable populations when external shocks hit. Increased spending and debt accumulation during booms may also lead to a loss of market confidence during commodity price busts, requiring a large fiscal adjustment or contributing to debt distress (refer to box 2.3 for more details on external shocks and fiscal consolidation). The implication is clear: fiscal strategies that save windfalls during economic upturns, such as commodity booms, and deploy those savings during downturns allow governments to respond effectively when shocks arrive.
Box 2.3  External Shocks and Fiscal Consolidation
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 69 (PDF page 93)]
Fiscal consolidation following a major external shock is particularly difficult and less likely to preserve growth. For example, consolidation episodes preceded by terms-of-trade shocks were significantly less successful in maintaining per capita growth rates near preconsolidation rates than episodes that were not preceded by such a shock (figure B2.3.1). This result reflects not only policy choices but also the persistent economic damage caused by the shock and the need for governments to support vulnerable households and economic activity before adjustment can begin.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 69 (PDF page 93)]
Consolidation is often delayed even after fiscal balances become unsustainable, which carries compounding costs. Where the primary deficit was significantly larger than what would stabilize debt, countries tended to wait three to four years before embarking on meaningful fiscal consolidation (figure B2.3.2; Di Lorenzo and Lacey 2024). Political and social constraints are particularly binding in the aftermath of a shock, but delay can compound the eventual costs. Where large sustainability gaps (that is, the primary deficit was significantly larger than what would stabilize debt) persisted for four years or more, the median debt ratio increased by 17 percentage points of gross domestic product. Growth also weakened: during periods of sustained fiscal unsustainability, average real gross domestic product per capita growth fell to the 32nd percentile of each country’s own historical distribution. For countries facing high borrowing costs and limited market access, these findings underscore the value of early, credible, and growth-conscious corrective action.

text:
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications | printed page 71 (PDF page 95)]
Establishing credible fiscal institutions and fiscal buffers. When a shock hits, the fiscal impact can be immediate and large, as spending needed to protect vulnerable communities rises while revenues fall. Governments can prepare for this tendency by establishing contingency reserves within the annual budget, natural disaster funds with clear rules governing their use and size calibrated to historical experience, and state-contingent debt instruments and other insurance mechanisms that transfer a portion of disaster risk to third parties (Polacek 2018). Well-designed fiscal rules can reinforce these buffers while allowing temporary, transparent flexibility during severe shocks. These instruments should be integrated into broader fiscal risk and debt- management frameworks. Contingent liabilities, including guarantees to state- owned enterprises, public-private partnerships, financial sector support, and disaster-related obligations, should be identified, monitored, and disclosed. Medium-term expenditure frameworks offer one powerful mechanism for translating these commitments into practice, aligning spending with strategic priorities and ensuring the planning horizon needed to address future shocks before they arrive (World Bank 2012).
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

Food Import Exposure, External Debt Burdens, and Healthy Diet Affordability
Food imports are an important channel through which external shocks can affect food and nutrition security. They are particularly relevant as countries face an uncertain external environment, with geopolitical tensions, weather-related shocks, trade disruptions, and volatility in energy and fertilizer markets posing continued risks to global food markets and prices (FAO 2026; World Bank 2026a). Such shocks may be especially difficult to absorb in economies with high external debt burdens. In countries that rely more heavily on imported food, such shocks can translate into higher domestic food prices, with potentially important implications for household purchasing power, welfare, and diet quality, given the substantial share of food in household consumption, especially in lower-income countries (FAO and World Bank 2018).
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

This section extends that analysis by examining food import exposure as one important source of vulnerability to external shocks, including the importance of food in merchandise imports, reliance on imported supply across food groups, and the diversification of import sources. It also examines associations between external debt burdens and changes

Food Import Shares in Poorer Economies Across the sample, which consists predominantly of LMICs, the share of food in merchandise imports generally declines as income per capita rises (figure 2.13, panel a). By contrast, economies with larger external debt burdens relative to exports also tend to have higher food import shares (figure 2.13, panel b).5
Both relationships matter for an economy’s capacity to manage food import exposure. Lower-income economies may have less room to absorb increases in import costs, and a high debt-to-exports ratio indicates that external debt is large relative to export earnings. During external shocks, higher import costs can therefore coincide with weaker economic and external buffers; export earnings may also decline, further increasing pressure on foreign exchange resources and raising the debt-to-exports ratio, even without an increase in the debt stock.
source: World Bank, International Debt Report 2026 (CC BY 3.0 IGO), 9781464823558.pdf

Import Reliance and Debt Burdens Across Food Groups Aggregate food import shares do not show how strongly the domestic supply of individual food groups depends on international markets. Net import reliance— net imports as a share of domestic supply quantity—varies substantially across the six food groups making up the Healthy Diet Basket (Bai, Herforth et al. 2025; Herforth et al. 2025). Among net importing economies, median reliance is highest for oils and fats, at 63.6 percent, followed by starchy staples, at 36.9 percent, and legumes, nuts, and seeds, at 34.1 percent. Median reliance is lower for animal- source foods, at 28.0 percent, and for vegetables and fruits, at 17.4 percent and 13.4 percent, respectively.

Figure 2.14 highlights economies where external debt stocks are at least 150 percent of exports, as a reference point based on the threshold applied under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Initiative,6 and where net imports account for at least 30 percent of domestic supply in a given food group.
